title: Acceleration
subject: Physics

English.simple_explanation: Acceleration tells you how quickly an object's velocity is changing.
English.detailed_explanation: Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken: a = (v - u) / t, where u is the starting velocity and v is the final velocity. Its SI unit is metres per second squared (m/s2). Because velocity includes direction, an object accelerates when it speeds up, when it slows down, and even when it only changes direction at a steady speed. Slowing down is often called deceleration, which is simply acceleration acting opposite to the motion.
English.everyday_example: A bus pulling away from a stop speeds up, and a bus braking slows down. In the language of physics, both of them are accelerating.

local_example.text: A bus pulling away from a stop, a bicycle freewheeling down a slope, and a boat changing direction are all examples of changing velocity.
local_example.appropriate_usage: Use as a general local-context draft only until reviewed; do not present it as a claim about a specific route, vehicle, or person.

common_misconceptions: An object that is slowing down is not accelerating.
An object moving at a steady speed around a bend is not accelerating.

observe_around_you.invitation: You need a bicycle, or any slope you can roll something down.
observe_around_you.what_to_do: Start from rest and pedal steadily. Count seconds and notice how your speed changes in the first second, then the third, then the fifth.
observe_around_you.what_to_notice: Your speed is still climbing even when your effort stays the same. Now stop pedalling and coast. Your speed is now falling while you do nothing at all.
observe_around_you.concept_link: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes, not the velocity itself. Coasting shows it clearly: you are still moving forward, but accelerating backwards, because friction and air are slowing you.
observe_around_you.safety_note: Choose an empty, flat, familiar place. Do not test braking near traffic.

think_question: A bus holds a steady speed of 30 km/h but drives around a bend. Is it accelerating? Why?

misconception_keywords: speed is constant so there is no acceleration
reasoning_guide.correct_feedback: Good reasoning: you used the fact that velocity includes direction, so changing direction changes velocity.
reasoning_guide.partial_feedback: You are close. Say what velocity includes besides how fast the bus is going.
reasoning_guide.misconception_feedback: Steady speed is not the whole story. Velocity also carries a direction, so ask what the bend changes.

challenge.question: A cyclist speeds up from 2 m/s to 8 m/s in 3 s. What is the acceleration, in m/s2?
progressive_hints: The change in velocity is 8 - 2 = 6 m/s.
Now divide that change by the 3 seconds it took.

quiz_questions.question: A car goes from rest to 20 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration in m/s2?
quiz_questions.hint: Divide the change in velocity by the time taken.
progressive_hints: Divide the change in velocity by the time taken.
Starting from rest means u = 0, so the change is just 20 m/s.
